Scales the red, green and blue channels using the chosen color components. White retains all channels; lowering a component reduces that color throughout the image.
Blends neighboring pixels using a ring-shaped kernel. Increasing the size spreads the effect farther and changes how small bright details are smeared.

Displaces the image with horizontal and vertical waves. Each axis has its own amplitude and wavelength: amplitude controls the displacement, while a shorter wavelength produces more closely spaced ripples.
Reduces the picture to a two-color rubber-stamp design. Threshold separates the colors, softness controls transitions and radius smooths details before the separation.

Creates a flowing distortion guided by brightness edges and colour differences. Displacement controls movement near edges, balance changes movement from across the edges to along them, and intensity adds colour-dependent displacement.
Recreates the image as scattered sand-like points over a chosen background. Point count and threshold control coverage and the amount of detail that remains visible.
Changes overall color intensity. Lower values move toward grayscale and higher values strengthen color; the tone-mapping option changes how the resulting color values are handled.

Resizes by removing or adding low-detail seams instead of scaling every pixel equally. Set the target width and height; an optional mask can protect a region or mark it for removal, but large changes may deform important objects.
Converts the photo to warm brown tones for an aged monochrome look.
Applies a selected shader preset and its exposed parameters. Choose a valid preset first; missing, invalid or failed shaders leave the image unchanged, so verify the preview before export.
Increases contrast around edges to make them appear sharper. Strength controls the effect; too much sharpening emphasizes noise and creates bright or dark halos.
Slants the image along the horizontal and vertical axes without applying a perspective projection. Set each shear angle separately; resizing expands the output bounds to retain the transformed image.
Blurs by shuffling samples around nearby pixels. Radius changes the spread and threshold changes which samples contribute, giving a more irregular texture than Gaussian blur.
Fades one chosen edge toward transparency. Set the fade width in pixels or relative to the image; absolute mode also offers strength control.

Uses Sierra error diffusion to represent intermediate tones with a pattern of pixels. Threshold changes the tonal split; grayscale removes color before dithering. Compare the grain pattern at full size.

Uses Sierra Lite error diffusion to represent intermediate tones with a pattern of pixels. Threshold changes the tonal split; grayscale removes color before dithering. Compare the grain pattern at full size.
Applies a fixed television-screen stylization. Use it for a quick retro effect without adjusting grain and toning separately.
Creates a pencil-sketch-like image with a fixed combination of tonal and edge processing. Use it for a quick drawing effect without separate line controls.
Partially reverses tonal values for a solarized photographic effect. The fixed curve produces unusual light-dark transitions without a threshold control.
Converts pixels according to a single threshold without spreading error to neighbors. Grayscale creates a black-and-white stencil; without it, color channels are thresholded.
Turns detail into a simple woven mosaic. Size determines the scale of the alternating pattern; larger values merge more of the source texture.
Suppresses broad shading to produce a flatter, sketch-like result. Kernel size sets the neighborhood used to remove shadows; it is not a freehand drawing tool.
Spreads sampled colors into marks or streaks. Shape, distance and angle set the marks, while density and mixing determine how strongly they cover the image.

Builds a repeating kaleidoscope grid with blended transitions between rotated image sections. Frequency sets grid density, offset changes the sampled region and blend controls the softness of the joins.
Combines blur, edge outlines and reduced color levels for a softer cartoon look. Blur size removes texture, threshold controls outlines and quantization sets the tonal steps.
Highlights image gradients with the Sobel operator. Line size controls edge sampling; the output emphasizes contours rather than preserving normal photographic colors.
Detects edges from horizontal and vertical brightness differences with a Sobel operator. Produces a contour image rather than sharpening the original photo.
Applies a built-in LUT with deep shadows, greenish middle tones and bright highlights. Strength blends between the original colors at zero and the full color grade at one.
Applies a built-in LUT with warm brown middle tones and softer highlights. Strength blends between the original colors at zero and the full color grade at one.
Brightens all three channels and mixes them slightly for softer, lighter colors.
Reverses tones around a chosen threshold for a solarized appearance. Moving the threshold changes which tonal regions are inverted and where bright contour-like transitions appear.
Largely exchanges red and blue while keeping green, creating a surreal palette. It does not draw a portal.
Draws a star-like sparkle at a chosen center. Adjust its radius, number of rays, color and amount; randomness varies the ray lengths.
Cross-mixes RGB channels with a slight warm bias. It changes the palette without adding flames or glow.
Distorts a selected circular region as if viewed through a spherical lens. Centre and radius place the lens, while refractive index controls how strongly it bends image details.
Refracts the image through a sphere centred in the frame. Radius sets the affected circle and refractive index changes the bending inside it; use the preview to choose the desired magnification.
Arranges repeated image sectors into spiral arms around the centre. Count sets the number of arms and intensity controls their twist, with negative values reversing the winding direction.
Breaks the image into spiral sectors and offsets them separately. Count sets the number of sectors, intensity controls the displacement and distortion adds rotation to the fragments.
Repeats the image inside itself as a receding spiral. Intensity controls the scale ratio between repetitions and distortion controls the rotation of successive layers.
Warps the image into a convex shape, stretching details for a curved-surface effect. Strength increases the deformation; this is a creative distortion rather than lens-profile correction.
Maps image brightness to magenta to yellow. This false-color palette replaces the original colors; useful for making tonal differences visible or creating a graphic effect.
Repeats progressively scaled image regions in concentric square bands, resembling a stepped lens. Intensity controls the density of the square bands.

Repeats the image inside itself in nested square or rectangular spiral layers. Intensity controls the scale ratio, distortion controls the twist and shape aspect stretches the pattern between square and rectangular forms.
Applies stack blur at the chosen processing scale. Radius sets the smoothing; a lower scale sacrifices fine detail to reduce processing work.
Builds a mosaic with staggered cells instead of aligned rows. Size controls the cell scale and the amount of detail retained.
Blends neighboring pixels using a star-shaped kernel. Increasing the size spreads the effect farther and changes how small bright details are smeared.

Overlays circles whose concentric rings stretch colours sampled from the image. Count and radius control the circles, layers sets the number of rings, seed changes their positions and intensity blends them with the source.
Expands a horizontal strip through the centre by stretching its sampled pixels vertically. Size sets the strip width and intensity controls the stretch.
Represents the picture with stroke-shaped mosaic elements over a chosen background. Size controls stroke scale; the background color fills the spaces between them.

Uses Stucki error diffusion to represent intermediate tones with a pattern of pixels. Threshold changes the tonal split; grayscale removes color before dithering. Compare the grain pattern at full size.
Maps image brightness to green to yellow. This false-color palette replaces the original colors; useful for making tonal differences visible or creating a graphic effect.
Mixes warm red and cool blue tones for a dawn-like color grade. It does not add a sun.
Twists a circular region around a movable centre. Radius controls the affected area and angle controls the amount and direction of the swirl.
Smooths with a tent-shaped weighting that gives closer pixels more influence. The value controls the spread of the blur.
Adds a colored crack texture. Density controls how closely cracks are spaced, relief changes their depth-like appearance, and channel selection limits where the texture is applied.
Turns regions into stained-glass-like pieces with visible separators and shading. Edge strength, thin separators and color controls determine how strongly the panes are distinguished.

Copies one side of the image and reflects it across a chosen horizontal or vertical centre line. Choose the source side and centre position; moving the centre away from the middle can reduce the output width or height.

Divides the image into tiles and stretches sampled colours into streaks within each one. Frequency sets tile density, balance changes the streak shape, variability changes displacement between tiles, and seed changes the arrangement.
Keeps a circular region clearer and blurs the surrounding image. Center X/Y and radius place the clear region; blur radius and sigma control the outer softness.
Remaps input tones with editable curves. Lift a curve to brighten that range or lower it to darken; separate channel curves also change color balance.
Creates a cartoon-like rendering with reduced color levels and dark outlines. Threshold controls edge detection, and quantization controls the number of tonal steps.
Extracts small bright details by subtracting the morphological opening from the source. Kernel size and shape determine which bright structures remain in the result.
Cuts irregular transparent notches into selected image edges without enlarging the canvas. Tooth height and spacing control the tear; save in an alpha-capable format to preserve the cutouts.
Maps shadows, midtones and highlights to three chosen colors. Use it for controlled three-tone coloring while keeping the original distribution of dark and light areas.

Approximates the color appearance of absence of blue-yellow discrimination using a fixed color matrix. Useful when checking whether a design relies only on color; it is not an individual vision assessment.

Approximates the color appearance of reduced blue-yellow discrimination using a fixed color matrix. Useful when checking whether a design relies only on color; it is not an individual vision assessment.
Maps image brightness to a vivid blue-green-yellow-red sequence. This false-color palette replaces the original colors; useful for making tonal differences visible or creating a graphic effect.

Maps image brightness to a cyclic palette with matching endpoint colors. This false-color palette replaces the original colors; useful for making tonal differences visible or creating a graphic effect.
Maps image brightness to a shifted cyclic Twilight palette. This false-color palette replaces the original colors; useful for making tonal differences visible or creating a graphic effect.
Rotates image details progressively around a chosen centre to form a whirl. Angle sets the twist in degrees and its direction, while radius limits the affected area.

Uses two-row Sierra error diffusion to represent intermediate tones with a pattern of pixels. Threshold changes the tonal split; grayscale removes color before dithering. Compare the grain pattern at full size.
Compresses the tonal range with the Uchimura curve. Exposure controls the brightness entering the curve; compare highlights and shadow detail. This cannot recover clipped source data.
Increases edge contrast using an unsharp-mask-style correction. Intensity controls sharpening; strong settings can amplify noise and create halos instead of restoring true detail.

Adds analogue-video-style distortion and colour misalignment for a VHS appearance. Strength controls the disruption and seed selects a different frozen phase of the pattern; the filter produces a still image.

Simulates NTSC and VHS signal damage, including colour bleed, tracking faults, tape wear, noise and ringing around edges. Start with amount and the main defect controls, then tune the detailed signal settings; amount zero bypasses the effect.
Changes color vividness with a vibrance adjustment. Tune the strength while comparing muted and already colorful areas; it is a global correction rather than a selected-color replacement.
Fades the edges toward a selected color to draw attention to the center. Start and end control where the fade begins and ends; choose black for dark corners.
Darkens and mutes the color channels for a faded vintage palette.
Maps image brightness to dark purple through blue-green to yellow. This false-color palette replaces the original colors; useful for making tonal differences visible or creating a graphic effect.
Creates a Voronoi-style crystal mosaic. Scale, randomness and grid shape control the cells; borders, stretch, angle and turbulence change their geometry and separation.
Rebuilds detail with a vortex-like mosaic pattern. Size sets the pattern scale; larger values emphasize the swirling cell arrangement over fine source details.
Boosts red and slightly reduces blue for a warmer overall tone.

Creates concentric ripples spreading from a selected point, as after a drop hits water. Radius limits the effect, wavelength controls ring spacing, amplitude controls distortion and phase shifts the wave pattern.

Warps the image with waves along both axes, as if viewed through moving water. Size sets the scale of the effect, while horizontal and vertical frequency and amplitude independently control wave spacing and displacement.
Connects weak edge pixels near stronger ones in an edge-processing chain. Use it with edge-detection filters; it is not a dead-pixel repair tool.
Interlaces horizontal and vertical strips into a woven texture. Separate strip widths and gaps determine the proportions and spacing of the weave.
Combines a whirl with inward or outward deformation around a selected centre. Angle controls rotation, radius sets the affected area and the sign of amount changes between pinching and bulging.
Adjusts the warm-cool balance with temperature and the green-magenta balance with tint. Use a neutral area as a reference; the filter does not automatically identify the correct white balance.
Maps image brightness to blue to green. This false-color palette replaces the original colors; useful for making tonal differences visible or creating a graphic effect.
Approximates tones with ordered pixel mixtures using the Yliluoma dithering method. The grayscale switch produces a monochrome pattern; this variant has no threshold slider.
Blurs detail outward from a selected center to imitate zooming during exposure. Center X/Y place the origin and blur size sets the strength.
Automatically detects and restores faces with GFPGAN v1.4, blending them into the original image. Strength controls the restoration amount.
Removes atmospheric haze with DehazeFormer-T. Best suited to outdoor photos.
Get instructions for a task and open the matching tools

Assistant uses a downloaded model to explain tools and settings. Open it from the main screen or the Assistant tab in a tool’s settings panel. Starting from a tool can include its selected files and current parameters in your question.
Choose a model in the chat and download it. If the Assistant button is hidden, enable Assistant in Settings.
Describe the result you need and any limits, for example “Compress these photos below 500 KB each” or “How do I keep a transparent background?”.
Read the answer and open a suggested tool or setting. Assistant explains actions; you apply them in the tool and check the preview before saving.

A follow-up can refer to the recent conversation. Only a short part of recent messages is included in each request; the complete chat is not an unlimited memory. Images from earlier messages are not passed to the model again.
State the tool, format or parameter you mean if the answer loses context.
Use Stop to interrupt generation. You can change models for the next request without deleting the conversation.
Start a new conversation when changing to a different task. Attach the image again when asking a new question about its contents.
Lite, Advanced, Max and three Vision models

The ordinary models answer questions about ImageToolbox using documented tools, settings and file metadata. They do not see attached image pixels. Model downloads and installed sizes are shown in the model selector.
Lite uses Qwen3 0.6B: start here for short instructions and devices with limited memory.
Advanced uses Qwen3 1.7B: a larger text model for more detailed explanations and comparisons.
Max uses Qwen3 8B: the largest ordinary text model. It needs more storage and RAM and may take longer to answer.

Vision models add image understanding: descriptions, captions, questions about visible contents and suggestions for editing a particular photo. They also answer text-only questions about the app. A larger model can handle harder requests but still makes mistakes.
Vision Lite uses Qwen3.5 0.8B. Choose it for simple image questions and the lightest Vision download.
Vision Advanced uses Qwen3.5 2B. Try it when Vision Lite misses details or gives an incomplete explanation.
Vision Max uses Qwen3.5 9B. It is the heaviest Vision option, intended for devices with ample free RAM and storage. Its larger capacity does not guarantee every detail is correct.

Downloaded file size is not the amount of RAM needed during a conversation. Loading the model, processing a photo and generating an answer also use memory. Response speed depends on the model, device and request length.
Use Lite or Vision Lite first to check responsiveness on your device, then compare the same request with a larger model.
Choose the smallest model that answers your task well. Delete unused downloads from the model selector to free storage.
If generation is interrupted or the app closes under memory pressure, use a smaller model, close other heavy apps and shorten the question.
Descriptions, captions, visible details and editing suggestions

Choose a Vision model before attaching a photo. The image picker accepts one photo, and the plus button stays unavailable while it is attached. The app prepares a smaller copy for analysis; the original file is not edited.
Tap plus, choose the photo and ask a specific question: “Write a short caption”, “What is on this image?” or “Which edits would improve this photo?”.
Remove the attached photo to choose a different one. For another question about the same photo, attach it again; earlier attachments are not reused as visual input.
Check small text, counts, names and other precise details yourself. Use OCR for extracting readable text, and open the suggested editing tool to apply changes.
Install, cancel, switch and remove local models

Assistant runs locally on supported 64-bit devices. Internet is needed to download a model; questions and attached photos are then processed on the device. Downloaded models remain available between app launches.
Open the model selector, check the download size and available storage, then download the model. Wait for verification to finish before using it.
Cancel an unwanted download in the model list. To free space after installation, delete that model there; switching models alone does not delete downloaded files.
Chat history is stored locally. Clear the conversation with the chat’s delete button. If the input is too long, shorten the request or start a new conversation.
Enlarge photos and illustrations with AI
RealESRGAN, RealESRNet, SRFormer, DAT2 and anime models

Upscalers generate additional image detail while increasing resolution. Their x2, x3 or x4 scale comes from the chosen model. This is different from ordinary resizing and cannot reliably reconstruct details that were never captured.
Filter the model list by Upscale. Try a photo model such as RealESRGAN, RealESRNet or RealWebPhoto for photos; use an Anime variant for line art and animation.
Compare the preview at a useful zoom. Look for invented texture, halos, changed lettering and overly smooth faces before processing a batch.
Use chunking when the selected model supports it and memory is limited. If the model’s output is larger than you need, resize it afterward.
SCUNet, FBCNN and models for specific defects

Noise, JPEG blocks, motion blur, banding and halftone patterns are different problems. A model trained for one of them can damage useful detail when applied to another. Start with one correction, then judge whether another is needed.
For JPEG blocks try FBCNN or a DeJPEG model. For grain try SCUNet or a denoising model; match Color and Grayscale variants to the image.
For blur, rain, halftone or banding, read the specific model description instead of using a general upscaler. FBCNN exposes a strength control for comparing gentler and stronger cleanup.
Check text, hair, fine patterns and skin at normal viewing size. Avoid repeatedly denoising the same saved image when it starts to lose texture.
DDColor, DDColor Tiny and DDColor Artistic
Colorizers predict plausible colors from grayscale contents. They cannot recover the original colors with certainty: clothing, objects and skin tones may differ from the real scene.
Select a Colorize model in AI Tools. Start with DDColor Tiny for a lighter model, or compare DDColor and DDColor Artistic on the same source.
Preview the whole image, then inspect faces and object boundaries for color bleeding. Clean severe noise or damage separately if it interferes with the result.
Save a separate copy and keep the original grayscale scan. Treat the new colors as an interpretation when working with archival photos.
Repair detected faces and control how much is blended back

GFPGAN v1.4 detects faces, aligns each one for restoration and blends the result into the source photo. Restoration can alter facial features, especially when the source face is small or badly damaged.
Choose GFPGAN v1.4 in AI Tools and generate a preview. The app processes detected faces; it does not need you to crop every face manually.
Lower Strength if eyes, mouth or skin become unnatural. Compare both the restored face and its transition into the original photo.
If the photo does not change, the face may not have been detected or Strength may be zero. Try a clearer source; keep the original when the restored identity looks wrong.

DehazeFormer-T reduces atmospheric haze and can restore contrast in outdoor photos. Haze is different from motion blur, defocus and digital noise, so this model should not be used as a universal sharpener.
Choose DehazeFormer-T in AI Tools and start with a hazy landscape or distant subject.
Check the sky, dark areas and color balance in the preview. Stronger contrast can also emphasize noise and make an already clear photo look harsh.
Save only after comparing with the original. Use Curves or exposure filters afterward if the overall tone still needs adjustment.
Straighten pages and remove document shadows

UVDOC Grid estimates page deformation and straightens a photographed document. DocShadow SD7K corrects uneven illumination and shadows. These operations prepare a page image; they do not recognize text or create a searchable PDF by themselves.
Use Document Scanner or Crop to isolate the page. Try UVDOC Grid when the paper is curved rather than simply rotated.
Try DocShadow SD7K for shadows crossing text or uneven lighting. Check fine letters, tables and pale markings in the preview before saving.
Pass the cleaned image to Recognize Text or Images to PDF. If the source is blurred or cropped, retake it rather than expecting cleanup to recreate missing text.
Arbitrary Style Transfer, MicroAST, AesFA and VGG19 Optimization

A separate style reference guides the textures and painterly appearance of each selected source image. Choose a style-transfer model and the reference image before previewing the result. Written image-generation prompts are not used.
Select a Style Transfer model, then choose the Style image. Source photos and the style reference have separate selectors.
Compare Arbitrary Style Transfer, MicroAST or AesFA when you need a quick stylized result. VGG19 Optimization iteratively adapts each image and can take substantially longer.
Adjust Strength and generate a preview. Check recognizable subjects and lettering before saving a batch with the same style image.
Check whether an image may be AI-generated
Compare detector estimates without treating them as proof

AI detectors estimate how closely an image resembles their training examples of generated or real images. The result is not proof of authorship or editing history. A real photo can be flagged as AI, and a generated image can be missed.
Choose an AI Detection model, select the images and run the check. This mode returns estimates instead of edited photos.
Read the score together with the verdict: 70% and above is Likely AI, 30% and below is Likely human, and the middle range is Uncertain.
Compare a different detector when a result matters. Compression, resizing and screenshots can change its estimate; use the original file when possible.

The catalog includes Mirage SigLIP2, LPX SwinV2, ConvNeXT Tiny, ResNet-50, AI vs Deepfake vs Real, CapCheck, Deep Fake Detector V2, AI Image Detect Distilled, Community Forensics and SMOGY. They use different training data and can disagree.
Start with a smaller detector to check speed, then compare a larger one on the same original file.
FP16 and FP32 variants describe number precision and file size, not a promise of more reliable AI detection. Compare their outputs on your images.
The app presents an overall AI score, including for models trained with several generated-image classes. It does not certify a file’s origin.
Automatic masks, portrait models and MobileSAM points

Background models separate a foreground subject from its surroundings. Available choices include BiRefNet, RMBG, InSPyReNet, U2Net/U2NetP, ISNet and MODNet. The best mask depends on the subject, edges and background; the biggest model is not always the best fit.
Open Background Removal and choose an automatic model. Compare models on hair, transparent objects and busy backgrounds instead of judging only the center of the subject.
Use MobileSAM point selection when you need to specify the subject: add points to keep and exclude areas, inspect the mask, then apply it.
Refine the result with erase and restore. Save to a format with transparency such as PNG; removing a background is different from filling an unwanted object with plausible content.
Paint the area to fill and compare it with the surrounding image

In Draw, Spot Heal can use downloaded LaMa inpainting instead of the OpenCV method. It fills a painted area using its surroundings. The result is generated content and cannot reveal what was originally behind an object.
Open Draw → Spot Heal, enable generative inpainting and download LaMa if prompted. Paint the unwanted object with a small margin around its edge.
Inspect repeated patterns, lines and nearby subjects. Undo and refine the mask if the fill distorts them; smaller, separate repairs are often easier to control.
LaMa settings let you limit processing resolution and choose worker threads. In AI Tools, Watermark Remover combines automatic mark detection with LaMa; always inspect what its mask removed.
Descriptions, reference photos, custom categories and people groups

Semantic photo search in Gallery and Embedded Picker uses its own search models, separate from Assistant models and AI Tools. It finds matching contents and organizes the library; it does not alter the original photos.
Turn on Semantic photo search in Search settings and let the app download the files and prepare accessible photos. File name search works while preparation continues.
Search by a description or choose Find similar photos. Use categories and the current album to narrow the results, or create a category from a description and reference photos.
Enable Group people for face groups, names and merge suggestions. Use the detailed Semantic photo search guide for thresholds, hidden groups and deleting local search data.
Review local usage and reset the counters
Usage Statistics summarizes recorded tool use. It helps you see which parts of ImageToolbox you use most. These counters describe app usage, not the contents or quality of your photos.
Open Usage Statistics and review the summary and per-tool entries.
Open the information dialog to read how the counters work before comparing them.
Reset usage statistics clears tool opens, save statistics, streak, saved data and top format. The app-open counter remains unchanged.
Find the components used by the app and their notices
The libraries screen lists third-party components used by ImageToolbox. A library license and a downloaded model’s license can be different; consult the relevant source when you need its exact terms.
Open Libraries and find the component you need.
Open its details to read the available description and license information.
For AI models, also open the model’s source link from its selector. A library entry does not replace the model’s own documentation.
Local models, image understanding, restoration, style, depth and detection

Depth Anything V2 offers Small, Base and Large models in Q4 and FP32. Depth Anything 3 also offers several sizes and precisions, including Mono Large. The app uses normalized relative depth for effects, not a calibrated distance measurement in meters.
Start with a Small or quantized model, then compare a larger version on the same photo if boundaries or thin objects are missed.
Use Custom depth map when you already have a matching map. It replaces model depth estimation for the effect; align it with the source photo and inspect the preview.
Remove the custom map to return to model estimation. Depth models work on the whole scene, so chunk and overlap controls are not offered for them.

Available results include the depth map, lens blur, background blur, portrait, color grading, depth edges, normal map, stereo, depth mask, cutout, focus color, fog and relighting. Controls change with the selected effect.
For blur, portrait, masks and cutouts, adjust Focus and Focus range while watching the subject edges. Focus selects a depth band, not a named person or object.
Use Strength for the amount of the selected effect and Light angle where relighting provides it. Stereo and normal maps are derived images, not recovered camera geometry.
Inspect hair, glass, sky and objects at similar depths. If the depth estimate is wrong, compare another model or provide a corrected custom map before saving.
The panel shows controls supported by the selected model. A missing slider does not mean the model is broken. Some tasks require the whole image or have a separate result panel.
Strength is available for FBCNN, style transfer and GFPGAN. Style transfer also needs a style image; depth models have their own effect controls and optional depth map.

Chunking is unavailable for tasks such as background removal, DDColor, face restoration, document correction, dehazing, depth, style transfer and AI detection. For them, reduce source dimensions or choose a smaller model if memory runs out.
Generate a preview before saving or sharing. AI detection returns a score and verdict instead of an image, so image effect controls do not apply there.
Tesseract, PaddleOCR v5 and PaddleOCR v6

Recognize Text offers Tesseract and two PaddleOCR providers. Their downloaded data and controls are different. The selected engine is also used when writing recognized text to a file, image metadata or a searchable PDF.
For Tesseract, choose the languages on the page and download the missing language data. Its language, page segmentation and engine options apply only to Tesseract.
For PaddleOCR v5, select a model matching the script, such as Latin, Cyrillic or East Slavic, and download it. Tesseract language selection does not configure PaddleOCR.

PaddleOCR v6 uses its Universal V6 model automatically instead of the v5 model selector. Download its files before working offline, then compare the same readable image across engines and proofread the output.
